title: Clinical and treatment-related factors influencing the development of radiation-associated sarcomas as a late complication in cancer survivors
summary:
Radiation therapy is a key pillar of cancer treatment; it helps fight tumors and alleviate symptoms in advanced stages of the disease. About one in two cancer patients receives radiation therapy at some point during their cancer journey. In many cases, it is part of the curative treatment for cancer. There are two types of side effects associated with radiation therapy. Predictable (deterministic) side effects: These occur in many patients once a certain radiation dose is reached, such as skin irritation. And random (stochastic) side effects: These occur in only a very small number of patients, and there is no fixed threshold at which they might occur. Nevertheless, as the radiation dose increases, so does the risk of damage to genetic material (DNA), which in very rare cases can lead to a new cancer. The side effects of radiation therapy can be divided into two categories. Predictable (deterministic) side effects: These occur at or above a certain radiation dose, such as skin irritation, and random (stochastic) side effects: Here, there is no fixed threshold at which they occur. Nevertheless, the risk of DNA damage increases with higher radiation doses, which in very rare cases can lead to a new cancer.

A very rare form of such radiation-induced cancers is radiation-associated sarcoma (RAAS). RAAS stands for “Radiation-associated sarcoma.” These tumors often develop years after the successful treatment of an initial cancer, such as breast cancer. RAAS is difficult to treat, and the prognosis is hard to determine on a case-by-case basis. It is particularly distressing for those affected that RAAS is a consequence of the therapy that originally cured them of the first tumor. 
This research project was launched to better understand the causes of RAAS. We suspect that several factors play a role in the development of RAAS.
 
As part of the TTRIS study, we aim to analyze the radiation therapy and treatment plans used for the initial tumor, as well as data on the treatment of radiation-associated sarcomas and on cancer incidence in the families of those affected. This will enable us to better assess the risk of developing RAAS. The goal is to maintain the proven benefits of radiation therapy for cancer treatment while further reducing the very low risk of developing RAAS. We will also compare the data collected here with data from the German Cancer Registries.
 
-    Analyzing the radiation therapy and treatment plans for the primary tumor can provide clues as to whether characteristics of the radiation used and other therapies contribute to the development of radiation-associated sarcomas. 
-    Surveys on cancer in the family provide important clues about a genetic predisposition that could indicate an increased risk for radiation-associated sarcomas. 
-    Comparing the data collected here with cancer registry data is important for verifying the quality of our data and examining larger population groups. 

Our goal is to better research radiation-associated sarcomas, detect them earlier, and perhaps even prevent them. We also aim to provide better advice and support to patients and their families in the future. 

Since RAAS are very rare, we collaborate with experts throughout Germany. We are also supported by patient representatives from the German Sarcoma Foundation (DSS). As part of our collaboration with other scientists, we are also conducting further research on RAAS. This is being done within the TTRIS-CSI project, which is funded by the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology, and Space (BMFTR). The study is part of the TTRIS-CSI research project. We can provide you with information about TTRIS-CSI, or you can find it at www.umm.de/ttris-cis/

interventions.name:
This is a prospective, non-interventional study.
The study-related measures are limited to data collection. No intervention takes place.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
-    There is a history of radiation therapy for a tumor with a known irradiation region. 
-    The sarcoma, as a secondary tumor, is located within the irradiated area or in anatomical proximity to it.
-    The time interval between radiation therapy for the first tumor and the onset of the sarcoma is longer than 6 months. 
-    The sarcoma has been confirmed histologically. 
-    The histology of the sarcoma and the first tumor is different.
Exclusion criteria:
The patient is not capable of giving consent.
